## Principle

Feedback control rests on a simple idea: measure the variable you care about, compare it with the value you want, and act so as to oppose any difference that appears. This chapter is anchored to one familiar example, the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid flows into the tank at a rate set by the process upstream, and out through a line fitted with a valve the control system can adjust. The material balance fixes the behaviour: whenever the inflow is greater than the outflow the level rises, whenever the outflow is greater the level falls, and only when the two flows are equal does the level remain steady.

The control loop therefore begins with a measurement of the level, which is compared against the set point, the value at which the level is to be maintained. The difference between the two is termed the error, and it is on the basis of this error that the controller decides how to move the outflow valve: if the level is too high, the outflow is increased, and if it is too low, the outflow is reduced. Because the action opposes the deviation that called it forth, the feedback is negative and the loop is self-correcting.

Under proportional control, the change made to the outflow is proportional to the error, with a consequence students often find surprising. If the inflow undergoes a sustained change, the outflow must change by the same amount for balance to be restored, yet under proportional action a changed valve position can only be maintained by a standing error. The level consequently settles away from the set point, at an offset that grows with the disturbance and shrinks as the proportional gain is raised. Integral action overcomes this drawback: while any error persists, the controller keeps moving the valve in the correcting direction, bringing the level back to the set point and eliminating the offset, since the new valve position no longer depends on an error to sustain it.

The simple model sketched above is a deliberately narrow one. It deals with a single measured variable and a single manipulated variable, it supposes that every element responds proportionally and instantaneously, and it ignores delays, limits of travel, and measurement noise altogether. The worked example that follows stays within this idealised picture, and the final part of the chapter turns to the question of where the picture ceases to be a faithful description of a real loop.

## Equipment

A practical loop is built from three functional elements: an instrument that measures, a controller that decides, and a final element that acts.

Measurement of the level is the job of a level transmitter. Depending on the application, a float or displacer may follow the surface directly, or a differential-pressure cell may infer the level from the pressure exerted at the base of the tank; either way, the instrument produces a signal that represents the level across the range over which control is required. This signal is the loop's only window on the process: everything downstream of the transmitter responds to the signal, not to the level itself, so any fault or bias in the measurement is acted upon as though it were real.

The controller accepts the measurement, holds the set point, computes the error, and generates an output signal in accordance with the control action that has been selected, whether proportional, integral, or a combination of the two. Its tuning determines how vigorously a given error is answered and how persistently it is chased.

The final element is a control valve installed in the outflow line, driven by an actuator that converts the controller's output signal into a stem position, working against the forces exerted by the flowing liquid and by the valve's own spring or air supply. Where the actuator by itself cannot hold the stem accurately at the demanded position, a valve positioner is added. The valve is also the point at which the loop's behaviour on failure is fixed in hardware: if the signal or the air supply is lost, the valve travels to its failure position, fully open or fully closed, and the choice between the two is made by asking which failure is safer, an overfilled tank or an empty one, rather than by control considerations.

## Worked example

Consider the tank running steadily, with inflow and outflow equal and the level at the set point. Now let the inflow step up to a higher rate and remain there, as when an upstream unit raises its throughput.

Initially nothing has yet happened to the outflow, so the inflow exceeds it and the level begins to climb. The transmitter detects the rise, an error develops, and the controller, acting proportionally, opens the outflow valve further. The outflow increases towards the new inflow, the climb of the level slackens as the two flows converge, and the level finally settles at a new steady value above the set point, where inflow and outflow are once more equal. The residual error is precisely the error needed to hold the valve at its new opening, exactly the offset the principle predicts under proportional action alone: balance has been restored, but at the wrong level.

Now introduce integral action. As long as the error persists, the controller keeps edging the valve open, the outflow rises beyond the rate that balanced at the elevated level, and the level is drawn back down towards the set point. The movement dies away as the level reaches the set point, because the error that was driving it has disappeared, and the loop comes to rest with the flows again equal, the level at the set point, and the valve held at its new opening by the accumulated integral term rather than by any standing error. The example bears out the principle step by step: the flow balance dictates the level, proportional action alone leaves an offset after a sustained change in the inflow, and integral action removes the offset by sustaining the new outflow without an error to do it.

## Limits

The simple model departs from reality first in its treatment of time. A real measurement is never instantaneous: transmitter, signal, and actuator each take time, and the process develops over time, so that by the moment the loop acts, the level it acts on has already moved. Dead time of this sort limits how aggressively a loop can be tuned, and a controller set up for a brisk response on the simple model will oscillate on the real tank.

The second departure concerns range. A valve can only open so far and can only move so fast, and a disturbance that calls for more outflow than the fully open valve can pass is beyond correction, whatever the tuning. In addition, the characteristic of a real valve is nonlinear, particularly towards the ends of its travel, so that the gain of the loop is not a constant but varies with the operating point to which events have pushed it.

The third departure concerns the boundaries of the problem. The model treats the tank in isolation and the inflow as an external event, whereas in an operating plant that inflow is the outflow of some other unit with a loop of its own, and the two loops interact. The model treats the measurement as though it were the level, whereas a noisy measurement is acted upon as though the level itself were jumping about. And the model assumes a self-regulating process of the kind described, whereas a tank emptied by a pump at a fixed rate integrates the imbalance, and the same settings produce a different response. The simple model, in short, is a statement about a single loop, a single variable, small movements, and an absence of delay, and it is trustworthy only within those conditions.

## Principle

Feedback control holds a chosen variable at a chosen value by acting against its deviations. The example used throughout this chapter is the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid enters the tank at a rate set by the process upstream, and leaves through a line whose flow the control system can adjust. The level is fixed by the balance between the two flows: the level rises while the inflow exceeds the outflow, falls while the outflow exceeds the inflow, and holds steady only while the two are equal.

The control loop measures the level and compares the measurement with the set point, the value the level is to be held at. The difference between the measurement and the set point is the error. The controller acts on the error and moves the outflow so as to reduce the error: a level above the set point calls for more outflow, and a level below it calls for less. The action opposes the deviation that produced it, which is what makes the feedback negative and the loop self-correcting.

Under proportional action, the movement of the outflow is proportional to the error. This has a consequence that the rest of the chapter uses. If the inflow changes and stays changed, the outflow must change by the same amount to restore the balance, and under proportional action a changed outflow is held only by a standing error. The level therefore settles away from the set point, by an offset that grows with the size of the change and shrinks as the proportional gain is raised. Under integral action, the controller keeps moving the outflow for as long as an error stands, at a rate set by the error; the level is then driven back to the set point and the offset is removed, because the outflow can be held at its new value with no error remaining.

The simple model behind these statements is narrow. It treats one measured variable and one manipulated variable, it treats the response of each part of the loop as proportional and immediate, and it says nothing about delays, limits of travel, or noise. The worked example stays inside that model; the closing part states where the model stops describing a real loop.

## Equipment

The loop has three working parts: a measurement, a controller, and a final element.

The measurement is made by a level transmitter. A float or a displacer follows the surface, or a differential-pressure cell infers the level from the pressure at the tank base; in each case the instrument delivers a signal that represents the level over the range the control is required to cover. The measurement is the loop's only knowledge of the process, and every later part of the loop acts on the signal, not on the level itself.

The controller receives the measurement, holds the set point, forms the error, and computes the output signal by the control action selected, proportional, integral, or the two combined. The controller is where the loop's behaviour is set: its tuning decides how large an output change a given error produces and how persistently an error is pursued.

The final element is a control valve in the outflow line, driven by an actuator that takes the controller's output signal and sets the valve opening against the force of the flow and the valve's own spring or air supply. A valve positioner is fitted where the actuator alone cannot hold the stem at the position the signal demands. The valve is also where the loop's safety behaviour is decided in hardware: on loss of signal or air supply the valve moves to its failure position, open or closed, and that position is chosen from the hazard of the tank overfilling or running dry, not from the convenience of control.

## Worked example

Take the tank at a steady level, with inflow and outflow equal and the level at the set point. The inflow then rises to a new, higher rate and stays there, as when an upstream unit raises its throughput.

At first the outflow is unchanged, so the inflow exceeds it and the level rises. The transmitter reports the rise, an error appears, and the controller, acting proportionally, opens the outflow valve. The outflow rises towards the new inflow. As the outflow approaches the inflow, the rise of the level slows, and the level settles above the set point, where the two flows are again equal. The standing error at that level is exactly the error needed to hold the valve at its new opening, and the offset in the level is the offset the principle states for proportional action: the loop has restored the balance, but at a level away from the set point.

Integral action is then added. While the error stands, the controller continues to open the valve slowly, the outflow rises past the rate that balanced at the raised level, and the level falls back towards the set point. The movement stops when the level reaches the set point, because the error that drove it has vanished, and the loop settles with inflow and outflow equal at the set point and the valve held at its new opening by the accumulated integral action. The trace matches the principle at each step: balance of flows fixes the level, proportional action alone leaves an offset after a sustained change in inflow, and integral action removes the offset by holding the new outflow without a standing error.

## Limits

The simple model fails first on time. A real measurement is not immediate: the transmitter, the signal path, and the actuator each take time, and the process itself responds over time, so the loop acts on a level that has already moved on. Dead time of that kind limits how hard the loop can be driven; a controller tuned for a fast response on the simple model will oscillate on the real tank.

The model fails next on range. The valve has a finite travel and a finite rate of movement, and a disturbance large enough to demand more outflow than the fully open valve passes cannot be corrected at any tuning. Near the ends of its travel the valve's characteristic is also nonlinear, so the gain of the loop changes with the operating point the disturbance has moved it to.

The model fails lastly on its boundaries. It treats the tank in isolation, with the inflow as an outside event; in a plant the inflow is another loop's outflow, and the two loops act on each other. It treats the measurement as the level; noise in the measurement is acted on as if it were movement of the level. And it treats the process as self-regulating in the manner stated; a tank whose outflow is fixed by a pump rather than by the level itself integrates the imbalance, and the same control action gives a different response. The model is a statement about one loop, one variable, small movements, and no delays, and it is reliable inside those conditions.
